title: Coordinated Use of Large Language Models in Academic Research
authors: Vladislav Marinov
abstract: This study proposes a methodological framework for the coordinated use of multiple large language models in academic research. Its central argument is that involving more models does not in itself guarantee more reliable results; what matters is how cognitive and verification operations are organised. The framework is based on seven principles (procedural independence, functional allocation, the diagnostic value of divergence, the diagnostic value of convergence, external verification, proportio

title: A four-level executable validation protocol for evaluating LLM-generated topology specifications of physics-based HVAC digital twins
authors: Younghwan Joo, Jeonghoon Han, Sanghyun Oh et al.
abstract: Physics-based digital twins of air conditioning, a principal energy consumer in manufacturing and buildings, can be generated automatically from a declarative specification of its equipment, connections, and sizing. Large language models (LLMs) now write such specifications from plain-language descriptions. Evaluations of these specifications stop at parse success, completed runs, or textual similarity, and cannot reject a model that converges in simulation but is physically wrong. In this study

title: SGLayout: Schema-Guided Closed-Loop Refinement for LLM-Driven Parameterized Layout Generation
authors: Siyang Chen, Yuan Pu, Yuhan Qin et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in parameterized layout generation via tool-augmented code synthesis. However, LLMs lack spatial awareness, making one-shot generation unreliable. While layout quality can be evaluated with established techniques, a critical gap remains: geometric-domain evaluation outcomes cannot be directly translated into actionable code-level fixes, trapping iterative refinement in blind refactoring. We propose SGLayout, a self-refining framework that

title: Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author
authors: Atrey Desai, Deniz Böloni-Turgut, Ty Brassington et al.
abstract: Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer "who wrote this?" at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who. The latest models (Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon) match trained detectors like Pangram while also explaining their predictions in natural language, and Opus 5.5 names the correct lab for

title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management
authors: Qiming Huang, Hanze Dong, Jipeng Zhang et al.
abstract: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these

title: Stop Going in Circles:Loop-Triggered Routing for System 1 Decision Agents
authors: Zeming Yu, Huamin Ma, Yingyu Chen et al.
abstract: System 1 decision models (represented by Jev) provide fast, low-cost action selection, but existing agent integrations do not reliably translate these local advantages into task completion. At certain points during execution, an agent may repeatedly select the same actions without making progress toward its goal. LLM-based policies offer strong reasoning capabilities that support planning within an agent, but invoking them at every step incurs substantial overhead. The effective coordination sho

title: Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting
authors: Yang Liu, Shengbo Tong, Xiyuan Chen et al.
abstract: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Building on ZhuLong, it enhances the task-level harness with API ret

title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress
authors: Congyuan Yu, Runping Tian
abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement throug

title: ProbeAgent: Principled Diagnosis of Agent Failures in Verifiable Environments
authors: Yue Huang, Yuchen Ma, Shuhang Lin et al.
abstract: Improving agents requires discovering where they fail and understanding why. An agent acts over multiple steps in a changing environment, so diagnosing its failures requires more than inspecting the final response of a large language model (LLM). The same unsuccessful outcome can arise from task difficulty or from an error the agent repeats across tasks. We introduce ProbeAgent, an automated framework that discovers agent failures, tests their proposed causes, and identifies shared failure modes

title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution
authors: Ziqing Wang, Hamid Palangi, Lili Zhao et al.
abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recurs

title: ChatAtom: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Molecular Dynamics Simulation and Visualization
authors: Trupti Mohanty, Ming Du, Mitchell A. Wood et al.
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation resolves atomic-scale motion and predicts the structural, mechanical, and dynamic properties of materials, making it cen- tral to materials design and discovery. Yet an MD study requires an expert-driven workflow: designing the simulation, writing reliable input scripts, executing them, and analyzing the results with separate tools. Here we present ChatAtom, a multi-agent large language model system that translates a natural-language request into a complete MD

title: What Helps Language-Model Agents Review Violent Video? A Controlled Comparison with a Human Evidence Reference
authors: Mohammed El Amine Mokhtari, Matei Mancas, Virginie Vandenbulcke
abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three inte

title: Coherence by Construction: Synthesizing CTI Knowledge Graphs and the Formal Limits of Coherence Validation
authors: Tanzimul Alam Fahim, Mohammad Arif Hossain
abstract: Synthesizing relational training data such as knowledge graphs with a large language model typically emits structured objects one at a time, which keeps each object valid but leaves the relationships between them ungrounded. We study an alternative paradigm, generation by simulation: rather than describing a relational artifact, we simulate a process that produces it and take the artifact to be its causal record. Language-model agents propose intent and a deterministic referee resolves outcomes

title: Beyond Demographic Discrimination: Benchmarking Normative-Descriptive Calibration in LLMs
authors: Radhika Bhargava, Shinibali Bhattacharyya, George Mihaila et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, where they must distinguish between normative reasoning (what should happen) and descriptive reasoning (what is likely to happen). Most fairness benchmarks evaluate demographic discrimination under a single reasoning objective, and none we know of tests whether a model treats the same item differently when asked to describe an outcome versus decide one. We introduce normative--descriptive calibration, the

title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF
authors: Yixuan Duan, Kexin Geng, Hanwen Xu et al.
abstract: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be

title: Your Judge Inherits Your Prompt: In-Context Label Bias in an LLM-as-Judge Is Directional, Not Symmetric
authors: Abdullah Ahmad, Ahmed J. O. Ahmed, Luca Citi
abstract: LLM-as-judge has become a standard way to score open-ended model outputs, yet the judge is itself a frozen language model steered by a few in-context examples, and such models are known to absorb the label balance of their demonstrations rather than treat them as neutral illustrations. We ask whether this label bias reaches an LLM judge used inside a multimodal (video question answering) evaluation pipeline, and what form it takes. Using a fully frozen generator-judge pipeline, we hold the gener

title: Windchime: an Audiovisual Installation with Audio-Language Model implementations
authors: Trent Eriksen, Celeste Betancur Gutierrez
abstract: Windchime is an audiovisual installation in which spoken language retrieves music and interactive animations from an artist authored corpus. A local Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model transcribes each prompt while an audio-language model (ALM) embeds it and retrieval over 406 audio stems returns a soundscape with live coded Strudel fragments that layer into audio output. Simultaneously each spoken input results in retrieval of interactive Three.js animation scenes each containing unique ta

title: Depth-Linked Residual Tokens for Multimodal Retrieval and Generation
authors: Jiangfan Zhang, Wentao Bao, Xian Wu et al.
abstract: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we in

title: Weight-Space Programming Writes In-Context Learning and Matches Fine-Tuning in Language Models
authors: Konstantinos Skianis, Aristidis Likas
abstract: Weight-space programming is a frontier language model's recently reported ability to read and rewrite another network's weights without gradient descent. We investigate how examples can provide a weight update so that a weaker language model performs the task with nothing in the prompt, and study what it edits. Our experiments cover six tasks, four frontier editors and three families of weaker language models, without the editors being told anything about in-context learning (ICL). In most runs,

title: Rethinking Full-Weight LoRA with Domain and Task Adapter Scaling for Question Answering over Portuguese Well Drilling Reports
authors: Luan B. Guerra, Diogo M. Paes, Marcelo N. Grimberg et al.
abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains remains challenging, particularly for technical documents such as Portuguese well drilling reports, where annotated data are scarce and domain adaptation may compromise instruction-following capabilities. Although Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is widely used for parameter-efficient adaptation, its scaling after training remains insufficiently explored. This study investigates the impact of LoRA adapter scaling on question answering over P

title: How Language Models Compress and Compare: Understanding Selection with Token Covariance Maps
authors: Moshe Eliasof
abstract: Many language-model tasks reduce to selecting among structured alternatives, yet we still lack a simple picture of how a decoder-only transformer organizes an entire selection prompt across depth. We introduce token covariance maps, a prompt-level geometric view that tracks how token positions co-vary in hidden-state space at each layer. title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
authors: Wei Jiang, Ziran Liu, Wei Wang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
authors: Qiang Zhou, Jianing Deng, Siyan Dong et al.
abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. title: How Long Will My Language Model Run? A Benchmark for Pre-Execution Runtime Prediction
authors: Ashish Molakalapalli, Kangda Wei, Haonan Duan et al.
abstract: Researchers submitting deep learning jobs to shared GPU clusters need runtime estimates to request time limits, choose hardware, and budget compute. Large language models (LLMs) offer a tempting shortcut: describe the job and ask. We introduce PreRun, a benchmark for predicting deep learning training and inference runtime from information available before execution. PreRun contains 801 training and 1,884 inference records of language and vision models collected on a GPU cluster, paired with work

title: Non-Expanding Gated Continued Fraction Architecture for Feedforward Layers in Language Models
authors: Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy et al.
abstract: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. title: Pharos: Learning to Control Rare Events at Scale
authors: Jiajun He, Jacky Chen, Weiliang Luo et al.
abstract: Rare events drive transformations across physics, chemistry and biology, yet predicting their mechanisms and rates remains a fundamental challenge. Here we introduce Pharos, a framework that learns to make rare transitions accessible while predicting how frequently they occur under physical dynamics. Through stochastic optimal control, Pharos jointly learns the probability of completing a transition and how to steer simulations toward it, allowing sampling and learning to improve one another. Ac

title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
authors: Shardul Bansal, Seth Schilbe, Jarrod Barnes
abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace data

title: Beyond Output Suppression: Mitigating Privacy Risks in LVLMs via Visual Intrinsic Privacy Erasure
authors: Xiangkui Cao, Jie Zhang, Meina Kan et al.
abstract: Large vision-language models can extract personally identifiable information from images, making privacy protection essential for their deployment in perception-oriented tasks. Existing targeted fine-tuning and model-editing methods usually suppress sensitive answers by aligning the model toward safe responses. In this paper, we show that such protection can be illusory: although the fine-tuned model refuses to disclose private information under normal decoding, privacy leakage still occurs in s

title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction
authors: Una Suman Kumar Patro, Sibangi Subhadarsani, Narendra Badam
abstract: Unplanned 30-day readmissions among patients with diabetes mellitus impose a substantial clinical and economic burden, yet most predictive models use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models parse unreliably. We propose a neurosymbolic multimodal framework evaluated on the public Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters; 7

title: KnowledgeClaw: Towards Agentic Knowledge Engineering via Omnimodal Hypergraphs
authors: Haoran Luo, Jiapu Wang, Linhao Luo et al.
abstract: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release

title: A Hybrid RAG Framework for Deceptive Review Detection: Integrating RoBERTa-LoRA, FAISS-Based Retrieval, and LLM Reasoning
authors: Andrei Kostin, José Ángel Diaz-Garcia, Karel Gutiérrez-Batista
abstract: The growth of deceptive online opinions poses a critical risk of misinformation and fraud. This paper proposes a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system to automatically distinguish spam reviews. The architecture integrates RoBERTa with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) classification, FAISS semantic vector retrieval, and a Large Language Model (LLM) for final reasoning. The system was evaluated across balanced and severely imbalanced real-world scenarios. Results demonstrate that five epochs of fi

title: A Capability Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Platforms in Regulated Enterprises
authors: Abbas Raza Ali, Muhammad Ajmal Siddiqui, Moona Zahid
abstract: Agentic AI platforms-systems in which LLM agents plan, invoke tools, retain memory and coordinate to change the state of enterprise systems-are being procured faster than they can be measured. Public agent benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses; enterprises buy integrated platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, and they buy them largely on the strength of vendor demonstrations. We report an industrial evaluation programme ("bakeoff") run by the

title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
authors: Ziyan Yang, Taiwei Shi, Jieyu Zhao
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and ind

title: DSFlow: A Neuro-Symbolic Data Workflow Agent with Statistical Diagnostic Guardrails
authors: Junfeng Nie, Xiaohui Chen
abstract: Data science workflows often require tools that presume non-trivial technical knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) reduce this barrier, but a gap remains between flexible general-purpose agents and statistically controlled pipelines. We introduce DSFlow, a LangGraph-based neuro-symbolic data-agent platform that combines reusable, LLM-selected skills with deterministic diagnostic guardrails. Skills provide extensible task knowledge. Symbolic validation can accept a proposed method, request cla

title: SailSearch: Agent-Assisted Discovery in Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Dhriti Verma, Kanthi Sarpatwar, Vinicius Lima et al.
abstract: We present SailSearch, a human-guided workflow for algorithmic research with two language-model agents, and report results on Market Split and maximum independent set (MIS). For Market Split, our randomized algorithm searches across multiple lattice bases, dividing computation between enumeration and continued basis reduction. Across ten random seeds per instance, it found the first reported CPU-only solutions to 18 of 33 previously open QOBLIB instances, solving 130 to 133 of the 156 benchmark

title: FinVeriQA: Financial Research Agents for Question Answering: Routing, Retrieval, MCP Tool Use, and Provenance-Aware Evidence Verification
authors: Meenakshi Rajpurohit, Anna Phan, Ravikumar Komandur Narayanan et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval an

title: An LLM-Agentic Framework for Intelligent Work Order Management in Industrial Maintenance
authors: Nianjun Zhou, Dhaval Patel
abstract: This paper presents an AI-driven framework, CodeReAct agent, designed to enhance industrial equipment maintenance through natural language (NL) interactions. The framework employs an advanced AI agentic approach to interpret human instructions, providing knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and work order recommendations. It identifies patterns and trends and predicts work orders by standardizing industrial data into business objects (BOs) and utilizing analytical function API calls

title: DVBench: End-to-End Benchmark for Real-World UVM Design Verification Agents
authors: Jiaru Qian, Jiawei Li, Xiaolong Hu et al.
abstract: Design verification (DV) remains a major bottleneck in hardware development, with large-scale verification using the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) being highly labor-intensive. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer new opportunities for DV automation. However, existing benchmarks primarily construct mutually decoupled subtasks, which deviates from the real-world workflow. In this paper, we present DVBench, the first end-to-end benchmark for Real-Wor

title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent
authors: Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Meng Tang et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant.

title: Large Language Models or AI Agents for English to Arabic Translation? An assessment on WikiEn-Ar190
authors: Fatima Zahra Iguenfer, Yousra Chtouki
abstract: This research investigates whether a large language model or an autonomous AI Agent performs better at translating from English to Arabic, which is considered a low-resource language. The authors introduce WikiEn-Ar190, a new dataset of 190 carefully selected Wikipedia articles from 18 different areas, which were created and verified by two native Arabic speakers to ensure that they accurately reflect both meaning and style. Using this dataset, the study evaluates the translation quality of GPT-

title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents
authors: Lipeng He, Yihan Wang, Jiawen Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). title: Semantic Context Handoff with On-Demand Evidence for Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Guolong Zheng, Chen Hou, Xu Yang et al.
abstract: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. title: Reducing Inference Cost of Coding Agents with Timeout Cascades
authors: Boxi Zhou, German Sviridov, Dmitrii Ustiugov et al.
abstract: AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. Yet, agentic AI comes at the cost of a tremendous amount of GPU compute resources, which limits its profitability and its viability at scale. In this paper, we investigate whether smaller, cheaper models can cut this cost without sacrificing accuracy. title: AutoPI: Taxonomy-Guided Adaptive Red Teaming for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
authors: Stavros Damianakis, Konstantinos Psounis
abstract: Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents
authors: Ziyuan Wang, Genliang Zhu, Xiaobo Chen et al.
abstract: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. title: SCAFFOLD: Toward Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport for Reusable LLM-Agent Skills
authors: Nami Cho, Shailja Gupta
abstract: An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
authors: Matthew Li, Albert Liang, Dilip Raj
abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We bu

title: EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality
authors: Yu Yuan, Ruizhou Ding, Shaoheng Fang et al.
abstract: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI,

title: In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents
authors: Ilker Oguz, Colin Christian, Christophe Moser et al.
abstract: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains

title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
authors: Rui Li, Liyang He, Zheng Zhang et al.
abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a

title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
authors: Lirui Luo, Kelong Mao, Xinwei Yang et al.
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consul

title: Learning to Read Events for Exact State Tracking with Frozen Language Models
authors: Jeonghoon Lee
abstract: Long event streams require identifying each change and applying the changes in order. We train a selector on a frozen language model to read each transition. With API-only access, we ask the model to list the transitions. An external integer register composes them in order. A confidence rule can flag uncertain updates or retain several candidates. title: VisAlloc: Allocating Visual Supervision for On-Policy Self-Distillation
authors: Haoran Xu, Tian Chen, Yuhe Wu et al.
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising approach to improving visual reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, not all samples benefit equally from privileged visual guidance, and uniform token supervision can dilute visually grounded signals. We propose VisAlloc, a dual-level framework combining sample-level visual filtering with token-level counterfactual reweighting. A fixed paired-teacher filter retains samples answered correctly from an evidence-centered

title: LLM-Guided Cyber-Physical Attack Path Identification in Smart Grids
authors: Amr Elshazly, Jesse Roberts, Rachad Atat et al.
abstract: Identifying high-impact attack paths in cyber-physical power systems is critical for improving grid resilience. Existing methods typically rely on either structural topology analysis or simulation-based cascading-failure models. Topology-based approaches capture connectivity but lack adversarial reasoning, while simulation-driven methods are primarily suited for offline analysis and are less effective for rapid evaluation of evolving attack scenarios. As a result, identifying realistic attack pa

title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning
authors: Zeguan Xiao, Zhuocheng Liang, Yun Chen et al.
abstract: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
authors: Prakhar Mishra, Bhavya Yajush Awasthi,  Tanuja et al.
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we

title: Chain-of-Thought Hidden States Reveal Task-Solving Directions for Direct Answers
authors: Houman Mehrafarin, Ioannis Konstas
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the performance of Large Language Models by eliciting intermediate reasoning steps. However, CoT is far from perfect: on some tasks, models perform worse than with direct-answer prompting, and on others they generate a few hundred tokens to reach the correct answer. title: MIRAGE: A Framework for Multi-hop Reasoning under Dynamic Knowledge Injection
authors: Heyang Xu, HanWen Hao, Haifeng Wang et al.
abstract: Multi-hop Question Answering (MQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and synthesize multiple pieces of evidence into a coherent reasoning path, which is essential for complex tasks. However, prior work on knowledge updating for MQA has largely focused on simple fact edits, overlooking a more challenging and realistic setting---\emph{Knowledge Injection}---in which the model must simultaneously accommodate both conflicting updates and entirely novel information. Under this setting

title: Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure
authors: Behrooz Tahmasebi, Melanie Weber
abstract: Test-time compute has emerged as a powerful way to improve the accuracy of language models at inference time, with scaling laws quantifying how accuracy improves with additional forward passes. Existing scaling laws, however, focus on repeated sampling from a fixed prompt, even though many tasks admit multiple equivalent representations of the same underlying problem. A graph does not depend on how its nodes are numbered, and a program does not depend on the names of its variables, yet language

title: Rethinking Fixed-Horizon Latent Reasoning
authors: Tianxiang Chen, Jingyuan Zhou, Weiming Yang et al.
abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. title: ReflectRec: Cycle-Consistency Preference Verification for LLM-based Recommendation
authors: Dae Kyoo Kim, Heejung Cho, Sungmoo Hong et al.
abstract: CoT-style LLM recommenders generate a natural-language preference note as a chain-of-thought prefix to ranking, but the note is trusted without verification, and the ranker never consults behaviorally similar users. We propose ReflectRec, organized around a preference-to-history round-trip verifier whose recall score serves as an operational signal of preference-to-history recoverability, enabling conditional regeneration for low-recoverability preferences and selection among regeneration attemp

title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Bangji Yang et al.
abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLM

title: VG-Steer: Visual-Geometric Policy Steering from In-Context Aligned Abstractions
authors: Arthur Bucker, Pramod Anantharam, Jonathan Francis et al.
abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy

title: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation
authors: William Fleshman, Joseph Lucas
abstract: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screen

title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models
authors: Huu Binh Ta, Alex Morehead, N. Benjamin Erichson et al.
abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and genera

title: NaviGATE: Noise-Aware Dual-View Generation for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
authors: Jie Peng, Yongxue Shan, Yongfu Zha et al.
abstract: Multimodal knowledge graph reasoning (MKGR) aims to infer missing facts by jointly exploiting relational structures, textual descriptions, and visual evidence. Existing embedding-based methods effectively capture graph topology, but their fixed multimodal representations are less effective for query-specific fine-grained semantic reasoning, while generation-based methods are vulnerable to noisy retrieval and may produce invalid entities. To address these challenges, we propose NaviGATE, a noise-

title: MECI: Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction for Multimodal Entity Linking
authors: Jie Peng, Yongxue Shan, Yongfu Zha et al.
abstract: Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. A pivotal challenge in MEL is capturing multi-level correspondences: the semantic consistency between mention-entity pairs and the complementary correlations across modalities. However, existing methods often suffer from element dominance due to their reliance on coupled interactions or coarse global aggregations. In response, we propose the Multi-Eleme

title: What the model knows but does not say: monitoring medical LLMs through verbalized thoughts
authors: Frederik Hauke, Jan Clusmann, Hanna Kreutzer et al.
abstract: Efforts to keep clinical language models safe have concentrated on what enters and leaves the model, but a manipulated model can return an answer that looks entirely ordinary. Here we show that the model's own internal state, rendered in plain language, exposes manipulations the output conceals. title: What Survives the Shift from Text to Pixels? Conditional Protection against Prompt Injection in Image-Rendered Documents
authors: Haoyang Liu, Yinong Xu, Zhe Lang et al.
abstract: Multimodal language models increasingly answer questions over external documents, exposing them to indirect prompt injection: commands planted in untrusted content to hijack the response. Rendering untrusted content as page images lowers attack success on average, leaving open which injected operations survive rendering, at what utility cost, and whether failed image attacks reflect unread commands or commands read but not followed. We pair text and page-image versions of 191 English question-an

title: NullTok: empirical-null token selection for training-free long video understanding
authors: Zhang Ziyue, Juwei Jian, Baiyang Song et al.
abstract: Long video understanding remains a daunting challenge for existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), mainly due to the large number of visual tokens accumulated in long videos. Currently, frame selection and token selection are two main paradigms for addressing this issue, both aiming to select relevant visual information to form a compact input for MLLMs. A natural approach combines these two paradigms by selecting frames before pruning tokens, but noisy frame-level relevance estimates

title: Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters
authors: Sanidhya Vijayvargiya, Rahul Lokesh
abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. title: Game-Theoretic Data Allocation for Expert Specialization and Routing
authors: Mark Lovett, Denis Lim, Soroush Vosoughi
abstract: Can the allocation used to train experts also predict which expert will perform best on a prompt? Such a connection would make the intended division of labor inspectable before training and allow the allocation itself to guide inference. We introduce InflEns, a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routes come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space. title: H3Remover: Reinforcing Video Object Removal without Paired Data
authors: Kangjie Chen, Xiangyu Li, Jinhao Deng et al.
abstract: Pretrained video editors possess rich removal and completion priors, yet may retain targets or alter unrelated content. We present H3Remover, which reinforces MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA for video object removal without paired object-free training targets. To discourage superficial edits such as recoloring, a target-removal reward favors calibrated depth changes consistent with revealing farther content. title: Compression Effects on Low-Resource Multilingual Translation
authors: Abbas Sani
abstract: We present a pilot study characterising the effect of post-training quantisation on multilingual machine translation quality and inference cost for three African languages - Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba - across three model families: a small general-purpose LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B), a larger multilingual instruction-tuned LLM (Aya-23-8B), and a dedicated multilingual MT model (NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B). title: Modeling LLM Reasoning Dynamics with Structural Representations
authors: Ilia Karpov, Andrey Atamanyuk, Dmitry Ilvovsky et al.
abstract: Language-model reasoning alternates between sustained activities and local operations. We study how this temporal structure predicts continuation and the computation needed to analyze it. T/E/S combines text, local events, and spans of activity. Across reasoning and information-seeking tasks, events and spans improve next-outcome prediction in 70 of 76 evaluation groups for a Transformer and 74 of 76 for Qwen with LoRA. title: Learning through Discernment: when a small language model learns from user feedback on the job, and when it decays
authors: Sirisilp Kongsilp
abstract: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $τ^2$-bench. title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
authors: Haoran Ye, Tianrui Huo, Hangzhen Li et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. title: What Majority Labels Hide: Annotator Disagreement and Model Errors in Multi-Dialect Arabic Sexism Detection
authors: Alaa Bazaid, Arkaitz Zubiaga
abstract: Judgements of sexism are subjective and may vary across communities, yet sexism detection datasets usually reduce annotator judgements to a single majority label, obscuring disagreement and how models behave on contested cases. We introduce MuDAS, a dataset of YouTube comments in Saudi, Egyptian and Moroccan Arabic, each labelled by three native speakers of its dialect, with the individual annotations preserved. title: Once Upon a Bias: Gender Stereotyping in LLM-Generated Children's Stories
authors: Sayumi Muthukumarana, Roshan Godaliyadda, Parakrama Ekanayake et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to create stories for children. Since bedtime stories can shape children's perceptions of social roles, this raises concerns about whether LLMs adapt narrative portrayals according to the intended recipient's gender. We conducted a large-scale study to examine gender stereotyping in LLM-generated bedtime stories. title: How Reward Gain Imbalance Shapes Ranking: Rethinking Rubric-Based Reward Aggregation
authors: Zhengyuan Fan, Zhonghua Wu, Tianyu Cheng et al.
abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning constructs rewards for aligning large language models with human preferences, typically by equally aggregating continuous scores that a judge assigns to individual criteria. However, scoring heterogeneity across criteria can distort candidate rankings. Existing work has focused on improving judges, learning criterion weights, or refining aggregation, whereas the interaction between scoring heterogeneity and ranking remains insufficiently understood. We formali

title: ReflectScene:MLLM-Guided Closed-Loop Diffusion for 3D Indoor Scene Generation
authors: Jiawei Shen, Jie Feng, Junpeng Zhang et al.
abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Shuaidi Wang, Zhuocheng Gong, Xuejie Liu et al.
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). title: LLMs Are Already Confidence-Aware Zero-Shot Classifiers
authors: Owen Cook, Xingyi Song
abstract: Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as text classifiers, but their labels are only useful when we know to what extent we can trust them. We compare black-box methods (verbalised confidence and sampling) with white-box methods that read token probabilities (P(True), and multiple logit-scoring methods using constrained generation). title: Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
authors: Takahiro Miki, Robin Schmid, Manthan Patel et al.
abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. title: A Verifier from the Past: Test-Time Compute for Time Series Foundation Models
authors: Arjun Choudhry, Aditya Narayanan, Raghav Mallampalli et al.
abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language models by spending additional inference compute to generate, verify, and select among candidate outputs, but this recipe has not transferred directly to time series forecasting. A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
authors: Yan Qiu, Yuanyuan Li
abstract: Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an additional downstream classifier. We propose Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), which uses binary safety labels to construct harmful and benign prototypes and makes predictions from relative prototype distances. JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation

title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
authors: Muhammad Rizky Wellyanto, Hajara-Yasmin Isa, Kexin Xue et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. title: Ground, Iterate, Trace: Decomposing AI Research Ideation
authors: Samson Yu, Qiran Zou, Jing Yu Lim et al.
abstract: Large language models have been widely used to generate plausible research ideas, yet it remains unclear what makes automated ideation effective and how generated novel proposals arise from prior scientific work. We introduce the Creative AI Researcher (CAR), an agentic framework combining literature grounding, iterative development and explicit conceptual operators. title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
authors: Zhiyu Liu, Xinyu Yang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. title: Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling
authors: Eugene Agichtein, Charles L. A. Clarke, Kaustubh Dhole et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
authors: Firas Spanioli, Yaniv David
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
authors: Oana Balmau, Saurav Banka, Jiaxuan Chen et al.
abstract: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. title: Enhancing Active Learning Performance with Initial Data Selection Based on Foundation Models
authors: Mohammad Mirzaee, Mehrshad Fallah Estalkhzir, Mohammad Reza Mohammadi
abstract: In active object detection, selecting the initial labeled pool is essential, especially in complex datasets with expensive labeling and low resource budget. This study presents an active learning framework designed to optimize the initial training cycle of active learning for the object detection task. title: LLM-Assisted Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization: Fusing Expert Knowledge with Numerical Data
authors: Dongjun Han, Mingyu Lee, Ikjin Lee
abstract: Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) reduces engineering design cost by combining inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) models with a few accurate high-fidelity (HF) evaluations and sequentially selecting designs to evaluate. However, when HF data are scarce, the LF-HF discrepancy is difficult to learn from numerical data alone, especially when physics omitted in the LF model makes it design-dependent. title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
authors: Xiaoyang Xing, Wenyu Dai, Xiaoliang Gong et al.
abstract: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models
authors: Johannes Hog, Neeratyoy Mallik, Steven Adriaensen et al.
abstract: Scaling laws are widely used to predict foundation model performance and guide compute allocation. However, tabular foundation models (TFMs) differ from conventional foundation models in that they are pretrained on virtually unlimited synthetic data from configurable distributions, while ultimately being evaluated on real-world datasets. title: Fast Bayesian Methods for Uncertainty Quantification in Sparse AI Evaluation
authors: Dario Deniz Ergun, Haohua Wang, Brendon Tao et al.
abstract: Estimating how an AI system will perform on a new benchmark need not require another large model. We use public evaluation counts to choose a weak Beta prior, then update it exactly from at most 31 revealed outcomes. The predictor uses no item semantics, pretrained weights, or inference API. Its single online evaluation in the AIMS competition returned a team-reported Brier ALC of 0.188477, a 24.6% reduction from the constant-0.5 reference. title: How Well Do Generalist CT Foundation Models Differentiate Liver Tumors?
authors: Yosuke Yamagishi, Tomohiro Kikuchi, Shouhei Hanaoka et al.
abstract: Generalist CT foundation models detect many findings with high performance, but their ability to differentiate detected lesions remains largely unevaluated. This retrospective study evaluated two generalist models, RADAR and Merlin, for differentiating liver tumors using a public single-institution multiphase CT dataset (517 cases: hepatocellular carcinoma, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, breast and colorectal cancer liver metastases, and hemangioma). title: LEDGE: An Efficient Simulator for Distributed LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Devices
authors: Zihao Wang, Ye Tian, Tajana Rosing et al.
abstract: Evaluating distributed large language model (LLM) serving on heterogeneous edge devices requires exploring diverse model partitions, device placements, and network conditions, making repeated physical experiments costly. An efficient simulator for edge LLM serving must support diverse, fine-grained placement configurations, capture runtime behavior, and accurately predict execution times while keeping simulation overhead low. title: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models
authors: Sachith Abeywickrama, Peiliang Gong, Emadeldeen Eldele et al.
abstract: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time.
